items.title: Earl King Interview, 1980-04-10
items.q: a friend of yours, Jerry Marksler

ctx.x: Usually, you can get a hook guitar player. If you're playing anything that is in the chord structure, you can be beat. Anything within the chord structure, you can play a little bit of a blues. The thing is, listening to the change of the name, the changes may move, but it's predominantly the same structure. Count Basie, Duke Kelvin, and I imagine hundreds of songs. I got rhythm, talking about the cyber guns, and I'm trying to come off that particular pulsation, or inverted at that point, you know.

I'm going to quote this to one person, when we started to define R&B, and I think there's another element that we touched on earlier, and a friend of yours, Jerry Marksler, who was president, vice president of Atlantic Records, who produced a number of R&B records in the 50s. One said that maybe it shouldn't have been called R&B, maybe it should have been called Rhythm and Gospel, instead of Rhythm and Blues. What do you think?

I think it probably would have took on a bad thing, because the Gospel, the people in the Gospel thing, was a problem, it was like they were priming on Great Charles, and a lot of things that, you know, on the borderline of some sense of the Gospel.
